title: Cyber Law in India — Introduction (IT Act, 2000)

content.overview: Indian cyber law is centred on the Information Technology Act, 2000 (as amended), which gives legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures, creates civil and criminal liabilities for computer-related wrongs, and establishes institutional machinery including the Controller of Certifying Authorities and adjudicating officers. Electronic evidence is governed primarily by the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (formerly the Evidence Act electronic-record provisions). Data protection is evolving under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 alongside IT Act residual rules.
content.glance: Ask: (1) Electronic record / signature recognition? (2) Civil (s. 43) or criminal (ss. 65–67 series) path? (3) Evidence under BSA s. 63? (4) Data protection overlap?
content.study:
Route by issue type: recognition of e-records, civil damage, cyber offence, interception/blocking, or evidence. Do not invent section text or case holdings.

No new case invented.

sections.heading: IT Act object
sections.body: Legal recognition of electronic records and digital signatures; facilitation of electronic commerce; civil and criminal liability for computer-related wrongs; regulatory institutions.

sections.heading: Key clusters
sections.body: ss. 2–10A (definitions, attribution, secure e-records/signatures); s. 43/43A (civil); ss. 65–67B (criminal); ss. 69–69A (interception/blocking); evidence interface with BSA.

sections.heading: Institutions
sections.body: Controller of Certifying Authorities; adjudicating officers; Cyber Appellate Tribunal history / current appellate path as amended — verify current institutional text.

sections.heading: Evidence
sections.body: Electronic records admissibility and proof under BSA 2023 (especially s. 63) — separate from substantive IT Act liability.

sections.heading: Data protection
sections.body: DPDP Act 2023 and residual IT Act/rules on sensitive personal data — concurrent regimes depending on the facts.

examples.title: Routing a hacking complaint
examples.body: Unauthorised access causing damage → s. 43 civil and/or s. 66 criminal; electronic logs proved under BSA s. 63.

hypotheticals.question: Is every online wrong only an IT Act offence?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. IPC/BNS offences, civil remedies and data-protection duties may apply concurrently; match the statutory path to the facts.

distinctions.title: IT Act vs general criminal law
distinctions.left: Computer-specific civil and criminal provisions under IT Act.
distinctions.right: General offences under BNS/IPC that may also cover fraud, cheating, defamation online.

misconceptions.trap: IT Act repealed all other laws for online conduct.
misconceptions.correction: IT Act is specialised; other statutes continue unless specifically displaced.
